technology.seoDescription: Explore Jalaranu's system concept, from shore facilities and computing modules to heat management, connectivity, and recovery.

hero.h1: Engineering starts with the right questions.
hero.body: Jalaranu explores the underwater lake datacenter as **one complete system**. Module placement needs to be evaluated together with power, networking, heat management, maintenance, and recovery.

architecture.h2: From shore interfaces to the underwater environment.
body: The concept architecture includes four elements: shore-based support facilities, power and communications connections, the computing module, and monitoring and operational management. Their relationships determine how the overall facility can function and recover.
Early visualisations use a truncated square pyramid. This is a design exploration; final geometry, materials, and specifications will follow engineering and test findings.
architecture.visualNote: A block diagram and cross-section showing logical connections, without coordinates or facility-security details.
architecture.imageAlt: Engineering concept figure of the truncated-pyramid module: front elevation, section A-A, roof framing plan, and watertight joint detail.
architecture.imageCaption: Dimensional engineering concept, not a fabrication drawing.

items.title: Heat management
items.body: **Water conditions, heat transfer**, computing loads, and the energy required by supporting systems.

items.title: Module integrity
items.body: **The ability of structures, joints, and system interfaces** to withstand the defined operating conditions.

items.title: Power and connectivity
items.body: **Service needs, redundancy options**, behaviour during connection failures, and recovery procedures.

items.title: Maintenance
items.body: **What can be monitored remotely**, when intervention is required, and how the module can be handled or retrieved.

items.title: Security and control
items.body: **Administrative access, event monitoring, key management**, operator responsibilities, and protection of physical and digital interfaces.

comparison.h2: Advantages need to be assessed against relevant alternatives.
body: Evaluation should compare the underwater lake concept with land-based solutions using equivalent service requirements, workloads, and assumptions. Relevant comparisons include land-based facilities with conventional cooling and water-based cooling, where applicable to the site under study.

Assessment covers energy, capital expenditure, operating costs, maintenance, connectivity, recovery, environmental effects, and end of life. Potential savings in one component do not in themselves demonstrate a lower total cost.

intro: The underlake concept is evaluated against three reference placements at equal service: a terrestrial facility, a hardened bunker, and an undersea deployment. Each trade-off below is an initial assessment to be tested, not a measured result.
placements.note: Initial framework assessment for discussion. Figures and rankings require measurement and site studies.

items.title: Terrestrial datacenter
items.body: The mature reference point: established supply chains, easy access, and proven operations. Its costs include energy-intensive cooling, land requirements, and the concentration of strategic data in a few urban corridors.

items.title: Hardened bunker
items.body: Strong physical protection for critical workloads. The trade-offs are high construction cost, more complex heat rejection, and a facility that is harder to scale than modular surface infrastructure.

items.title: Undersea datacenter
items.body: Proven at sea by Project Natick: ocean water removes heat without mechanical cooling. But the maritime threat surface includes submarine cable interception, anchor drag, and contested jurisdiction, with saltwater corrosion and difficult access.

items.title: Underlake datacenter
items.body: A lake is not a small ocean. Inland waters sit inside domestic jurisdiction, beyond submarine reach, in quiet freshwater near hydropower and existing communities. Open questions remain: thermal and ecological effects, seismic exposure, acoustic hardening, and retrieval procedures.

body: The concept can be evaluated for dedicated computing, storage, or particular infrastructure requirements defined by an organisation. The suitability of each use case must be established through requirements assessment and test evidence.
A use case mentioned here is not a statement that the service is already available or approved to handle sensitive data.
